body:
Is the memory measurement API cross-process as well? I guess it has to be if it can encompass multiple agent clusters. It's not entirely clear from its description how it's scoped.

If A embeds B embeds A, and outer A has incremental, inner A would still have to have COEP as well, right? Same for popups?

At a high-level, I worry about creating more categories of APIs beyond "Requires isolation" and "Doesn't require isolation". The developer messaging becomes (even more) complicated, and we get into line-drawing exercises for particular aspects of particular APIs around the margins that seem like distractions. 

At a lower-level, the threat model that I think we're assuming with COEP (and COOP) is one in which frames aren't process-isolated from their parents, as we need to support Chrome on Android, Firefox, and Safari in the medium-term. In those browsers, it's not clear to me than an implementer's selection of a set of realms to reveal is going to be a robust defense against leakage.

I'm sympathetic to deployment concerns, and some in-between state may well be justifiable in the short term (while noting that I'm not sure this kind of complexity is something we want to keep in the spec past the initial deployment challenges). One tweak to the proposal that would make me a little happier with it would be to restrict the looser policy restriction to same-site resources. That is, `example.com` could embed `widget.example.com` without an explicit CORP declaration (subject to the other caveats you suggest above), but could not do the same for `widget.not-example-at-all.net`.

> Is the memory measurement API cross-process as well?

No; it is per JavaScript agent, since it inspects JS heaps. Thus the danger is if you can get non-CORP-opted-in content into your agent. (For example, via `<script src="https://bank.example/useful-info.json"></script>`.)

Incremental COEP would protect against this, even if it doesn't protect against getting non-CORP-opted-in content into your process.

An additional bit of protection is that , the implementation can choose to not return information for a given realm inside the agent. So if there are some incremental-COEP realms in the agent and some with no COEP at all, then we could spec it to require that any realms without at least incremental-COEP would be omitted from the results.

> If A embeds B embeds A, and outer A has incremental, inner A would still have to have COEP as well, right? Same for popups?

This is a little abbreviated for me. Are A and B pages? (With some guard against infinite recursion?) Origins? Sites? Same-site origins? I'm not sure how to conceive of this scenario... If you could restate this with URLs I'd be much appreciative.

> At a lower-level, the threat model that I think we're assuming with COEP (and COOP) is one in which frames aren't process-isolated from their parents, as we need to support Chrome on Android, Firefox, and Safari in the medium-term. In those browsers, it's not clear to me than an implementer's selection of a set of realms to reveal is going to be a robust defense against leakage.

Right. The issue I'm pointing out is that there's another class of APIs besides ones that need process isolation. They instead need per-agent "everything is CORP-opted-in" guarantees. Currently, the only way to get that guarantee is with `COEP: require-corp`.

`COEP: require-corp` is intended for a stronger purpose, of ensuring that everything in the _process_ is CORP-opted-in. And meeting this stronger purpose, including in browsers without site isolation, requires the recursive restriction. But the proposed `COEP: require-corp-incremental` would give the per-realm guarantee, regardless of whether or not the browser has site isolation.

Let me know if I'm making sense :).

> The issue I'm pointing out is that there's another class of APIs besides ones that need process isolation.

I note that you skipped the portion of my response where I suggested that creating this additional classification risks both confusion and arguments about line-drawing (similar, actually, to the discussion we're having right here about COOP/COEP). So, I'll assert it again. :)

I think I can agree that the memory API and `SharedArrayBuffer` are _different_, while suggesting that the difference is in degree, not kind, and that they can be reasonably stuffed into the same box along with other things that are similarly different in degree. For example: WebPerf has some great paint timing APIs coming up. They likely have subtly different properties than the memory API, and therefore a different risk profile. Should we create another variant of COEP to tune towards the (narrower? broader?) set of risks those APIs specifically pose? As I'd find it difficult to justify an arbitrary number of categories; I think I'd prefer to err on the side of having fewer, broader buckets.

(I'd also reassert the claim that whatever we decide on this proposal, this kind of complexity isn't something we want to keep in the spec past the initial deployment challenges. Would you agree that the challenge here is one of short-term deployment, rather than long-term desirability?)

There are two related aspects that may also be worth considering here:
- If we move to a world where COOP+COEP are encouraged as a best practice and potentially become default at some point in the (distant) future, there is a lot of merit to making them simple. Saying "you adopted COEP, but it's the wrong COEP so no `SharedArrayBuffer`/nice lock icon for you" would probably be a bad experience for developers.
- There are relatively few providers of iframe-based widgets on the web, or at least there are many fewer of them than individual sites. My guess is that if we're worried about third-party iframes blocking the adoption of COEP, it may be better for the platform to focus on convincing the -- relatively few --  providers of such widgets to make them play nicely with COEP rather than work around that problem. Giving them an easy way out ("just use `require-corp-incremental` to get the memory API and we'll update our widget sometime in the future!") may make it more difficult for sites that need `SharedArrayBuffer` to get their vendors to make their widgets fully compatible.

The scenario I meant is roughly equivalent to https://a.example/1 embedding https://b.example/ which embeds https://a.example/2.

I tend to agree with Mike that there still are issues here as when b.example does not have COEP but is in the same process, there will be leaks.

In offline discusisons ,@ulan raised the good point that it's best to conceptualize this proposal as part of the spectrum, from report-only to full enforcement. That is, "incremental COEP" would be best done by websites as "report-only for subframes; enforce for this frame".

How do people feel about the proposal from that perspective? Sites would do `COEP: require-corp-incremental` + `COEP-Report-Only: require-corp`.

I think this addresses some of the assertions around classification risks and line-drawing. That is, the spectrum already exists, where sites start with report-only and eventually tighten to full enforcement; and this just lets sites do so in a way that involves a more-gradual step function.

> I'd also reassert the claim that whatever we decide on this proposal, this kind of complexity isn't something we want to keep in the spec past the initial deployment challenges. Would you agree that the challenge here is one of short-term deployment, rather than long-term desirability

Although I agree that the challenge here is one of deployment, I'm not sure I'd call it "short-term". Deployment is a long-term concern, and not something I'd see getting any easier over time.
I think the issue is not so much with allowing for gradual deployment, but with handing out favors before isolation is complete.

I am worried that a spectrum of isolation, where each step on the spectrum gives you an increasing number of features, is going to be hard to understand for developers.

I can see the proposal working for gradual deployment, but you shouldn't be able to gain access to anything until you have full deployment of COEP.
Thanks all for the discussion. It seems like there isn't a lot of interest in a spectrum of capability-granting here, so we'll withdraw the proposal.
